strengths: The paper addresses a clear research need: identifying an approximately accurate Pareto set over a continuous design space using costly, noisy evaluations. Researchers in Bayesian optimization and active learning have an identifiable reason to be interested.

The algorithm thoughtfully combines confidence regions covering entire cells, inherited confidence information, and a refinement-versus-evaluation rule. Its intuition, phase descriptions, and illustrations make the central approach understandable.
Studying both information-based and metric-dimension-based sample complexity is useful, and the multi-output GP formulation allows objective correlations to influence inference.
The experiments include 10 sampled functions with five runs each, four competing methods, and a tree-depth study. Reporting runtime alongside accuracy exposes an important computational tradeoff.
weaknesses: Necessary—correct or withdraw Proposition 1 and its claimed separation between the bounds. Appendix C obtains a lower bound containing T times a factor involving the squared amplitude at index T. Positivity and monotonicity do not keep that factor bounded away from zero, so the claimed Omega(T) conclusion does not follow. Keeping independent amplitudes bounded away from zero would create infinitely many points separated in the GP metric, conflicting with compactness and the assumed Hölder bound. The assertion that a suitable metric exists does not resolve this incompatibility.

Necessary—repair the confidence calibration supporting Theorem 1. The stated V_h contains log(h^2) despite including h = 0. Moreover, substituting the chosen u from Corollary 1 into Lemma 7 produces 2h log N, whereas V_h contains only h log N. The supplied union-bound argument therefore does not establish the stated simultaneous probability guarantee. These formulas and their consequences for the algorithm need correction before the claimed 1−δ guarantee is adequately supported.

Necessary—resolve the time-index argument in the dimension bound. Lemma 14, equation (31), uses the fact that a parent was previously refined to bound its current confidence-scaled posterior uncertainty. The refinement condition held at the earlier time, while β increases subsequently; the displayed implication is unjustified. A proof using the inherited confidence rectangle at the actual refinement time may repair this. Algorithm 1 also computes the pessimistic Pareto set before constructing the current rectangles on which its definition depends.

Necessary—make the experimental metrics mathematically consistent and establish what was actually computed. Section 7.1 describes accuracy by checking whether a predicted point is ε-dominated by a true Pareto point. Even a severely suboptimal feasible point can satisfy this, so it does not establish membership in Z_ε. The coverage description also treats ε-domination and 2ε-domination as equivalent. Provide precise formulas and correct the results if needed. Table 2 should report accuracy and coverage separately; their average can conceal failure of either requirement. Assessing the confidence guarantee additionally requires the frequency of runs satisfying both set-level conditions.

Necessary—qualify the practical performance claims. Experiments cover one input dimension, two independent squared-exponential objectives, and one noise/target-accuracy setting. The fastest variants set V_h = 0 at a chosen depth, removing the within-cell uncertainty protection used by the theorem. Their guarantees must be distinguished from their observed performance. Table 3 also shows a substantial tradeoff: the theoretical-depth version takes over 15 hours, while the 27-second variant has MSE 40×10^−6 versus qNEHVI's 10×10^−6 at 40 seconds. These results support narrower, setting-specific conclusions rather than general superiority.

Optional improvements: Higher-dimensional and correlated-objective experiments, a controlled comparison with uniform discretization or budget-limited ε-PAL, and clearer reporting of confidence-interval construction would strengthen practical guidance. These extensions are optional if the empirical claims are appropriately restricted.
